utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, if you're ready to continue your cross-examination, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's talk about the issue of the return of the Serbs. In paragraph 10 of your witness statement, you say that in April 1998, you strongly supported the plan and programme of refugees return to Croatia. And in paragraph 24, you mention an intensive programme of return of refugees and displaced persons. Now, that's three years after Operation Storm that these intensive programmes are implemented or discussed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the process of talks about the return of refugees began back in Dayton in November 1995. The first thing that was agreed was the Erdut Agreement on peaceful -- on the peaceful reintegration in of Croatian Podunavlje. And then in January 1996 I visited Belgrade, and with the foreign minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Milan Milutinovic, I started talks about the principles of protecting private property and the return of refugees, and we issued a joint communique in Belgrade. In May 1996, I proposed to Belgrade a bilateral agreement on the protection of minorities that included the turn of refugees. Several years later that proposal was accepted. Then on the 1st of August, 1996, during talks of heads of state and foreign ministers of the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the so-called Athens Declaration was adopted. Its main points were the protection of property and the return of refugees. Then in August I signed in Belgrade an agreement on the normalisation of relations between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which inaugurated the principle of protection of property of both physical and legal persons, and it also regulated the issue of the right of refugees to return, and it was only then in 1997 that main agreements were reached with the UNHCR. And finally in the beginning of 1998, the preconditions existed for such a plan and programme. Prior to that President Tudjman and the Croatian parliament adopted the decision on amnesty. Many trust-building measures and security-building measures needed to be put in place for that plan to be implemented. As for the speed with which all this developed, we drew on the experiences of other countries and the experience of the UNHCR, and they believed that our pace was very reasonable and that we took these steps at the right time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic. When you talk about the fact that UNHCR said it was a reasonable pace, Ambassador Galbraith testified here that only enormous pressure of the US and European Union made you and Mr. Tudjman agree on paper that Yugoslavia had to accomplish these steps in relation to the return. Do you agree that it was the enormous pressure from the US and European Union that forced you to seriously think about these programmes?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Galbraith had frequent talks with me. We talked both as statesmen and as friends. It's true that he put pressure for this to happen as soon as possible. However, I needed no pressure from Peter Galbraith; on the contrary. I myself was making efforts and worked for this. You must not forget that there were various opinions within the government. Whether it was the right time, not for the return of refugees, Serb refugees, as such, but whether the time was right in terms of the general atmosphere and the security of these refugees when they return. In these discussions I was helped by the position of Peter Galbraith, and I valued them greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's talk about another government, not the US government but the French government, and you agree with me that also the French government had concerns about the property loss, famous property loss, and concerns about the issue of the Serbs returning to -- to the Krajina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have 65 ter 7478.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is a note of a meeting between you, Dr. Granic, and French Ambassador Gaillarde on 19 September 1995 in Zagreb. And I'd like to show you first the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, at least I have a problem that it's not shown on my screen. I don't know how about my colleagues. Now it's shown. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember meeting Ambassador Gaillarde on the 19th September in Zagreb, Dr. Granic?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that I see this signature of my chef de cabinet, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 2. In English -- sorry, page 2 in Croatian and page 3 in the English. I want to read out what ambassador Gaillarde said or how he's quoted: "Ambassador Gaillarde thanked the minister for seeing him at such short notice and stressed that he had been given an instruction by his government to present a bilateral verbal demarche because of the concerns felt in Paris caused by frequent and identical reports made by various observers, humanitarian organisations, the ECMM, and the UN, about frequent case of endangering private property and persons in the recently liberated areas. In addition, he expressed concerns about various legal acts and administrative acts and project related to the return of Serbs, especially the one announced -- especially the one announced on 4 September, which leaves only 30 days for the refugees to register for the return. They are afraid that this decree means actual disposition. Friends of Croatia are therefore wondering whether the Republic of Croatia is really prepared to accept those who want to return because things sometimes look as if everything is being done to prevent their return." Then there is a piece of information about the visit of the president of the republic, and then in the second paragraph you answer that it was decided to extend the deadline for those who wanted to return and the parliament will also adopt it. Now, this is again a clear indication from one of your friends that things are going wrong in Croatia in relation to the return of the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for showing this record of the talks between me and the French ambassador. I must stress that a clear distinction has to be made between two things. One thing is the return of refugees, and the second thing was the protection of the enormous amount of property that suddenly became the target of criminals, looters, robbers in various groups. And when the Croatian government make the decision to take over that property for management and administration, it was the first time we were handling such a problem. There was not even much international experience with this sort of thing. There were all sorts of ideas, totally unacceptable, somewhat acceptable. And finally it was decided to place this property under protection. That's what our lawyers suggested. The term of 30 days was not designed to prevent the return of Serbs, because realistically speaking, there were no conditions at the time for a mass return of the Serbs. I tried to describe the timeline of all the steps taken for the Serbs to return. At that time, only individual family reunions were possible, not return on a massive scale. However, we took on board very seriously all the suggestions of the international community, such as those of Mr. Galbraith and Mr. Gaillarde. In this instance we said -- I said that we are going to accept these suggestions, that the deadline needs to be postponed. I must emphasise that four months later in Belgrade, at a press conference and jointly with Milan Milutinovic, the Yugoslav foreign minister, we said that all the refugees who were not responsible for grave violations of international law may return and that private property is protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2670.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, do you agree with me that if you make these public speeches or these negotiations with Mr. Milutinovic to press conferences, all these efforts on paper are worthless if President Tudjman and others around him publicly say that it would be impossible for the Serbs to return to the place where their families lived for centuries?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to avail myself of the opportunity to say in my answer the following: President Tudjman was a historian and a statesman at the same time. There is a clear distinction between the two personalities. I know that best as his foreign minister and his close associate. In all that I was doing, I had his support. Without him, I would not have been able to do anything. Tudjman the historian is something different. He frequently addressed the international community, from various ambassadors to Presidents Clinton and Chirac, and presented his positions as an historian concerning the relations between Croats and Serbs and Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. He said that to everyone who wanted to listen. However, Tudjman as a statesman was a pragmatic man who throughout, until his illness, abided by the recommendations of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, this happens again and again that you put a question which allows the witness to comment on matters which may be slightly related but which are not a real answer to your question. Why not ask the witness whether he's aware of such statements and then ask him on the basis of those statements. Then we know the context of the statements. We know the exact text of the statements to the extent it is available, and then to ask whether this would or would not undermine any commitment on paper, because that's apparently what you would like to know. And we now know that President Tudjman was an historian and statesman, but an answer to your question, we have not got.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps this is not the first that time this happens, not only yesterday, but today as well. I think that it would be appropriate that if you ask whether something is a short period of time or three months and you get a lengthy answer, that you'd guide the witness to your question again and to ask him to respond to that question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, could you please carefully listen to what exactly Mr. Waespi is asking you and to start with -- with giving an answer to that question. And if Mr. Waespi wants to know more or background, then of course he'll ask for more information. If at the end of your testimony you think that very important matters have not been brought to our attention, you will have an opportunity to add whatever. But at this moment I invite you to focus on the question when answering it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for your guidance, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Occasionally, Mr. Granic, I try to lift my hand, but I will put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we move to 65 ter 7501, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a press report that relates to an interview Mr. Tudjman gave to a German magazine called "FOCUS." Do you know the German magazine "FOCUS"? Did you read it at that time?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I followed "FOCUS," among other publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it's dated 4th of September, 1995. And if we go just to the last part, second page in English and second page in Croatian. Last question. The interviewer asks: "Can the 150.000 displaced Krajina Serbs go back home?" "Tudjman: If the Krajina Serbs wanted to stay home, they would never have left in the first place. The return of all of them is virtually unthinkable."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have the witness -- it's not on the B/C/S side. If he could be shown the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I apologise. I hadn't noticed that. Yes, we have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "In any case, this does not lie in the interests of a normalisation of Croatian-Serbian interests, but we will adhere to human rights and permit the Krajina Serbs to return in individual cases." Now, did you read this interview with Mr. Tudjman in "FOCUS" at that time?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not discuss this interview, but I can comment off-the-cuff. These are Tudjman's historical estimates based on the amount of people who did not wish for a Croatian state, the amount of people who participated in the insurgency, and the number of people who had committed grave crimes, that it was unthinkable. That's Tudjman's historical evaluation, which proved to be right to a great extent. However, Tudjman as a statesman and I as foreign minister worked exclusively on the basis of international law, international treaties, and everything that was needed to achieve the return of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, there is no qualification in President Tudjman's answer about war criminals. The question of the interviewer was about the 150.000 displaced Krajina Serbs. And President Tudjman, whether as an historian or statesman, publicly, in a German newspaper, said that: "The return of all of them is virtually unthinkable. In any case, this does not lie in the interests of normalisation of Croatian Serb interests." That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Could we please place in time that piece of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 4th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This period was a time when there were still plans for an attack to be launched from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia against the Republic of Croatia. It was a time when terrorist groups that would come to Croatia were publicly mentioned, the time when the so-called government in exile was established, and its goal was to launch terrorist attacks. So in other words, we should consider the period at which this was stated by President Tudjman. In my capacity as the foreign minister, as soon as the Erdut agreement was reached, I believed, and I received support from President Tudjman for that, that I should make efforts to have the Serbs who were refugees return to Croatia, and I really worked devotedly about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, could I ask you one question. You put this in the context of danger and attacks still to be considered. Could you tell us where in the words reported to have been the words of Mr. Tudjman any reference to this as a reason for at that moment not all the Serbs returning is found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is my interpretation of Tudjman's statement. He did not consult me, nor did I consult him, nor did I read this statement at the time, but I know his line of thinking at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I asked you where in the text you find a point of reference which would support this part of your interpretation that it -- that this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have never read this interview, so I cannot answer this question, except for the last quotation. I don't know. I haven't read the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in that last quotation, where do you find a reference that Mr. Tudjman may have been hinting at the threat of an imminent attack or terrorist activities which would temporarily --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this answer given by Mr. Tudjman, one cannot see that. I do not see it here. As I said, I explained the context of the period, but I don't see it here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour. JUDE ORIE: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2671.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit P2671 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to move on to the next document which is 65 ter 7473.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Dr. Granic, that's a meeting between the president and the prime minister Nikica Valentic, other people, on the 24th of April, 1998, a meeting that you did not attend. And I'll read a relevant part on page 3 in English and page 5 in Croatian. And the issue at stake between President Tudjman and Mr. Valentic is an incident, a resent incident in Bosnia where Serbs had prevented some Croats from attending mass, and President Tudjman says: "They attacked him, and they wouldn't allow the Croats attend the mass ... therefore, I think that the developments in Bosnia are good for us, because they will become aware how silly their request is that we should have all Serbs return to Croatia. How can you return all those Serbs to Croatia ..." Now, you weren't at the meeting. Were you aware of comments to that nature President Tudjman said?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this meeting. I did not attend it, so it's very difficult for me to comment on it. But I do know that Mr. Nikica Valentic was not the prime minister at the time. He was prime minister until the month of August 1995, and at this point in time he was not the prime minister. However, I do know that in the month of April 1998 there were big discussions about the plan and programme for the return of refugees and that there were differences within the Croatian government, not whether the return of the Serbs should be allowed but whether this was the right time for their return. There were different opinions voiced, and at the cost of resigning my position in the government, I requested from President Tudjman that he should support the plan for the return of refugees, and President Tudjman finally did support my position. I believe that it was quite democratic to discuss. There were various opinions voiced, but eventually I got the support of President Tudjman for the plan for the return of refugees, and this was probably part of the discussions about the return, but I am not aware of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But I suggest to you that this quote from President Tudjman in explicit terms reveals what his true intentions were in relation to the Serbs. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked with the president on many occasions. He believed that a return en masse would not happen because many Serbs - and time proved him to be right - did not wish to recognise Croatia as their state. That was what Tudjman believed as an historian, and he often repeated that. However, Tudjman as the statesman, and that was most important, supported all the plans that I have talked about, let me not mention them again, and this is a historical fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have an objection. The objection is before we put it into evidence, we get these transcripts and what somebody said at a private meeting. But I believe the burden is on the Prosecution to tie the transcript to some act of the government or some policy or something on the ground. That's their 90(H) obligation. And if that's case, then let's put it to a witness who is clearly -- here has relevant information and knowledge, but we're not talking -- we're not trying people for, you know, what somebody said in a private meeting, but, rather, for something concrete, and I believe they have a burden to now tie this to something to show that the policies that the witness has testified about in fact were not implemented or other policies were implemented or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness here came to testify and did testify about these plans to allow the return, about the will of the Croatian government, about the meetings they had the international -- internationals. And it's the position of the Prosecution that it is only on paper that there was no will from the Croatian government to implement, to invite the Serbs back, and this goes to support this opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2672.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2672 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you, Dr. Granic, had, as early as September 1995, some doubts about the return of the Serbs as well. And I'd like to show you a document that's already in evidence. That's P2540, a meeting of 9 September 1995. And I'm interested in English page 11 and Croatian page 27. And the context is that you, Dr. Granic, and Mr. Zuzul talked to the president about Mr. Bildt and discussed, you know, his relationships with the Serbs and others, and you also discuss international media. And then you say as follows: "That's right --" in the middle of the English -- "I have used the opportunity to explain one thing more. The Figaro and La Croix and everyone was there about the question of Serbs and their departure, that in this respect it's not realistic to expect those participating in fighting to return. They cannot return. They won't return. Their families, they do not want to return. Besides, Martic has announced a guerilla warfare to at least 50 years. We must consider it. Therefore we cannot have this factor of instability again. I wish to say that it is possible to use our brains in defending our standpoint." Now, do you remember having made this comment to the president in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it is very logical. It is completely correct. At the time when Martic announced that there would be guerilla warfare for another 50 years, those people who had killed 14.000 people and wounded 36.000 and who had taken part in the fighting, I said that it was not realistic that all of them would return, and I think that this was a quite logical statement from my part, and I think that I also this in public to the media in the same period. So put it precisely. Those who had participated in the fighting, it is not realistic that all of them should return. And this was precisely what was going on. President Tudjman and the Croatian parliament adopted the law on amnesty and abolition, but it was logical that it was not realistic that all such people should return, and I do not see anything in this that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I noticed that after 80 per cent of your answers you're seeking eye contact with the accused. That is not common for a witness to do, and I would certainly not encourage you to continue to do that. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to 65 ter 7471, and this is a meeting of 11 August 1995, in which, Dr. Granic, you were present, and you were discussing the upcoming election.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we move on to another transcript, is there a point that the Prosecution wishes to put to the witness about the last passage? He just was asked, did you say this? And then we don't have the Prosecution putting its case, whatever the case was, on the excerpt. What's the point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He asked an explanation. Apparently Mr. Waespi is exploring the attitude of political leaders during this period of time, that is, from before, but mainly after Operation Storm on their attitude to Serbs remaining, and if they have not remained on the territory of the former RSK, what efforts were made to make them return in view of the claims that they were welcome to remain living there, that they should not leave. And as a consequence he's exploring the -- I would say the -- to what extent these were expressions of what really was on the mind of those who spoke these words. That's what Mr. Waespi is exploring, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, and -- and I outlined what other people said, and I went on to say that the witness himself had doubts about that. And there's a lot of cover, Mr. President, and I would really like to move on and not be interrupted by Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you asked a question more or less, rather than raising an objection. If you want to raise an objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is an objection, Mr. President. It's an objection that we're moving through this case without the Prosecution putting its case to the witness. While I understand your comment, Mr. President, I didn't understand that that's the case of the Prosecution. So hence the confusion that you're understanding one thing; I believe Mr. Waespi is attempting to put something else. I certainly didn't understand that the issue is -- concerns the Serbs who remained in Croatia, as you've put it, but, rather, the issue was the return of those who left. And all of this is precisely the reason why I believe the Prosecution should put to a witness what their case is and not leave it open to interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I did not consider exploring these -- this attitude as being -- as being -- I did understand it as being a factual element in the case that is put by the Prosecution. But, Mr. Waespi, it wouldn't damage - I would say, it would perhaps even be good - if you explain to the witness what your case in this respect is to the extent it is not yet clear to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, I put to you that there was no will by the Croatian government to get the Serbs who had left for whatever reason in the aftermath of Operation Storm back, and you were among these people who had serious doubts about whether it would be realistic to invite the Serbs back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, now what is the Prosecution's case exactly in this respect? I can imagine that -- and as I said before, that the fact you're exploring may shed some additional light on -- but isn't it true that it's the case of the Prosecution that Operation Storm was an instrument to expel the Serbs rather than -- and that an obstruction for their return may have some meaning in this context, but these accused are not charged with obstructing the return, but, rather, they're charged or they are accused of joining in an exercise to drive them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is correct. It shows the intent. It corroborative of the element of intent, that we say they expelled the Serbs, and we have discussed that yesterday about this international reactions, again the corroboration, and this shows that the Serbs didn't leave on their own, and now the Croatian government makes all these efforts to invite them back. It shows the intent of what was in the mind of the JCE members before Operation Storm was launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say the events after they left which are indicative for -- the attitude of the political, military, and other leaders is indicative for what they had on their minds during Operation Storm when Serbs left, and as the Prosecution puts it, that they were -- through Operation Storm they were forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. In particular since the defence is that there was no JCE because the Croatian government, you know, made all these appeals, come back, all these programmes, and we say this is just not the reality. That's the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was actually going to raise then the objection. I'm glad that's on the record, but now given that Mr. Waespi has put Mr. Granic's comments in the context of the mens rea overall of a JCE, that must mean that he considers that Mr. Granic was part of it. Given that the comment now is indicative of intent or mens rea of before and during Operation Storm, we have not yet heard the case put to this witness about the existence of a JCE before or during Operation Storm and what he knows about it. And I was going to raise the issue at the break that under 90(H) he has now put him in the JCE. He needs to put his case to him about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever you may submit at this moment the Chamber does not see that Mr. Waespi is under an obligation to further put or to put in further detail its case in relation to the testimony of this witness and this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on to the next exhibit, I'm not sure I announced it yet, 65 ter 7471, a meeting - I think I might have discussed that - involving the upcoming elections. And this is on page 14 in English and page 64 in B/C/S. The president says as follows: "Moving on to item 3. The Presidency of the Croatian Democratic Union as the majority party has issued a decision to call an election in the autumn. In this connection all the necessary legal preparations need to be put in place, and one of the important decisions is to prepare a list of members of national minorities - not only Serbs, but all the national minorities - in these parts." Ivan Milas: "Establishing the number, that is a better way of putting it." President: "Yes, establishing the number, yes." Then in brackets: "(In order to protect the rights)(laughter)." Now, Mr. Granic, do you remember having attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly attended it, it's visible in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember the laughter after the protection of the rights of the Serbs and all the national minorities were discussed?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the details, but I'm not surprised. It is certain that at the meetings of the VONS -- and I said also when the issue how to protect the property was discussed, there were unacceptable ideas voiced, the less acceptable ones and more acceptable ones. So not everything that was said at the VONS meetings is wholly writ, nor were all the people who discuss this thinking the same about the strategic interests of Croatia. But we have to emphasise what the point in time was. It was the period immediately following the conclusion of the Operation Storm. It was a moment at which it was very probable and possible that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would launch an attack against Croatia. It was also a point in time when there was absolutely no chance at that moment that someone would return in an organised manner. So at that point in time when the president made the decision to slate the elections, a comment like this was also made. In my view this comment was certainly inappropriate, and I do not support it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Therefore, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit 2673.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2673 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to move to a meeting between President Tudjman and Croatian ambassadors of the 18th August 1995, and this is 65 ter 4103.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, discussed here are, among other things, public and international media perception of Operation Storm and its aftermath. Now, Mr. Granic, I don't see a reference, although there is one, actually, later in the document. Do you remember having been present?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should show that to me so I could see it. It says here that I attended it so I probably did. But I was a foreign minister for seven years and another two and a half years under a different president, so a total of more than nine years, and I attended numerous meetings. I see my name here at the beginning, so it's certain that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic. Let's move to page 30, and in English and in Croatian it's page 52 out of 58. Now, President Tudjman says, and the sentence starts in English at the end of page 29 in English: "But in practice the essence of the problem is that it would be normal that Banja Luka belongs to the west part, and Tuzla to the east. And then the problem would be resolved, because it's not the issue of a demarcation between Croatia and Serbia, but between the west and Russia. And Russia openly wants to expand to the west as much as possible. It's not only unpleasant for Croatia to have Serbs in Banja Luka and on the west like we have them within 30 kilometres of Zagreb, but it's unpleasant for the west as well." Do you remember this quote by President Tudjman to the Croatian ambassadors?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you think that's an appropriate comment from the head of state about a minority in one's own country to call them -- to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We can't get the B/C/S screen -- I think the transcript should be shown to him in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It's page 57 out of 58. Yes. That's the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't see the words "Banja Luka" on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry, 52. I misspoke. 52 in Croatian. Yes. The comment starts at the very bottom "Prema tome."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So please read these first three lines, and then we move on to the second page in Croatian. Go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really see the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we're now at the top of this page where it continues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I comment now? It's true that President Tudjman as a historian had certain thoughts about the strategic interests of both the east and the west, but I must stress that as the foreign minister, I was the main negotiator on behalf of Croatia with the US in Washington Agreement and the Split Declaration and Vienna Accords. And in all these talks, Croatia was the most constructive player and partner for the west in stopping the war and achieving peace, and President Tudjman supported me in this all the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not going into that. My question was related to this comment of the head of State of Croatia talking to his ambassadors, ambassadors to the world, including you, saying that: "It's not only unpleasant for Croatia to have Serbs in Banja Luka and on the west like we had them within 30 kilometres from Zagreb, but it's unpleasant for the west as well." Do you think that's an appropriate comment?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a comment of President Tudjman, but you must bear in mind, sir, the time when it was made, the brutal war, the crimes committed in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you must realise that at this time horrible crimes were still happening, and the horrible aggression of Milosevic, Karadzic, and Mladic was ongoing. Tudjman is talking within that context. It was not peacetime. It was still the time of a brutal war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, you were actually in cold sweat when you were listening to the speech President Tudjman gave in Karlovac when he told the Serbs who do not accept the Croatian state not to come back anymore. Isn't that correct? That's what you said in your book.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At that time, I was the foreign minister, and my entire thinking was primarily about Croatia's relations with the world. President Tudjman was head of state. That's when he started his electoral campaign, and he put it very precisely: Those who do not accept the Croatian state. And he also said that there were torchings and crimes on our part that must stop. In that case it was not convenient for me as the foreign minister that he should speak about Serbs at all, except to say that we need to prevent crimes after Operation Storm. However, Tudjman must have been talking, carried away by the realisation that approximately 90 per cent of the population of Croatia was thinking along the same lines, that around 30.000 people in split were appealing to him to resolve the problem of Vukovar, which he promised he would do in a peaceful way. But certainly I as the foreign minister was thinking more about international talks. And for me diplomacy was the highest priority, and that meant that not one more word must be said that could offend our friends in the world.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last thing he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, you're invited to repeat the last words you said. I read to you what is now at the transcript: "... and that meant that not one more word must be said that could offend our friends in the world." What did you say following the phrase I just read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that I said those who were the target of Tudjman's message, namely Serbs who did not accept Croatia as a state, did not really care at all about whatever Tudjman may say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So are you saying that you were sweating cold because of the image of Croatia that could be tarnished by the comments of President Tudjman? You did not care about, you know, how the Serbs who might be listening - after all, they were also addressed - to this speech by President Tudjman, about how would feel about their head of state talking about them?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I devoted a number of years of my life to accommodating displaced persons, refugees, and the return of the Serbs. And at least twice in my career I risked my entire career because I fought for the return of the Serbs, and I offered my resignation even to President Tudjman for the sake of this. I wanted every person who was exiled from Croatia to return, but of their own free will, which is the fundamental principle of the UNHCR. Refugees must be returning of their own free will. I'm the last person whom you can accuse of not caring. I cared. I cared for every individual Serb to return, everyone who wanted to, and I said many times. All of these are historical documents from the Dayton Accords and the talks on the normalisation of relations, and, finally, the plan for return of refugees. I succeeded. And finally every Serb was enabled to come back to Croatia, everyone has guarantees for their own private property, and I can say that I did succeed in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Actually, I wasn't asking about your concerns, but let's move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, if you ask the witness whether he had -- was in cold sweat because he didn't care, you are asking him about his feelings at that moment, and then if he explains that, you can't say, "I wasn't asking about your concerns," because you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to the next issue. This is Grubori. You were, I believe, asked in chief already about the incident of Grubori, and we have now D1812 in evidence, which you have been shown by Mr. Misetic. If we could call D1812, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. If I remember well, my examination-in-chief has never touched the issue of Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise as well for Mr. Misetic who showed the document to the witness. It's -- it was 65 ter 7486, and I believe it's now D1812.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is not the document, I don't believe, that Mr. Waespi's looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Perhaps let's focus on 65 ter 7486. And hopefully we have a B/C/S translation. Otherwise, I'll read briefly the key issues. This is an Associated Press document. Date's 28 August 1995. Location, Zagreb. "The new footage taken by the UN in southern Croatia shows Serb houses in flames and two Serb civilians slain in their homes." Then the village of Grubori is mentioned. Then we have a Mr. Flynn saying that almost every structure in this hillside village is in flames. And then we come to you, Dr. Granic: "Following a meeting with European union diplomats on Monday, Croatian foreign minister Mate Granic called the incidents isolated events which express the frustrations of people whose property was entirely destroyed. "Granic told diplomats that the government shortly would issue precise data related to Croatia's four-day blitz offensive to retake most rebel-held land." Now, do you remember the incident of Grubori and that you made a comment stated or picked up a Associated President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that. It was established yesterday that the comment was unrelated to Grubori, and I think it's misleading to present this witness as stating that this comment was related to Grubori.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm fine to ask him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we have two -- Mr. Granic is reported and questions were put to him to put clearly, and, of course, to put Grubori in the context of a four-day blitz offensive needs at least further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can ask the witness directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's not repeat any questioning that has occurred already at an earlier stage of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could move to P602, please. P602 should be a letter by Elizabeth Rehn to Dr. Granic. If we could move on to the next page, please. Yes. That's the letter I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, this is a letter from Elizabeth Rehn the Special Rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights, and it goes to you. And she talks about the Grubori case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could move to the second page in Croatian as well. If there is one. Yes. Here we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Granic, do you remember having received a letter from Elizabeth Rehn in relation to the Grubori events?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this letter is fairly detailed, if you recall the letter or you can briefly go through it. It discussed --

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It discusses the number of civilians killed, states that the entire hamlet was set ablaze, discusses the fact that a group of Special Police had been observed, the time of the incident, registration plate numbers, and Ms. Rehn is requesting information in paragraph 2 on page 2 of the actual letter. And in Croatian it's also the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. REHN ASKS
utterances.text: "Will you please let me know the identities of the persons who used these vehicles?" And Ms. Rehn asks other questions in this respect. Now, I take it you remember that you did respond to Ms. Rehn's letter. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. When I received that letter I talked to my associates, and I asked the chief of the section for human rights in my department to ask for an official report from the Ministry of the Interior. I had heard before that that a incident had occurred in Grubori, but in the Croatian press it was described as a clash with terrorists. So until I received the letter from Elizabeth Rehn, not much attention was given to it. So I asked for an official report, and based on that official report I answered the letter pursuant to the official information provided by the Interior Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So by the moment you received the letter 27 February 1996, not much attention was placed on it, despite the fact that there were public international media report about that as early as late August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, I was foreign minister. I dealt with the most important talks about war and peace, both on Bosnia and Herzegovina on the process of peaceful reintegration, or normalising relations with Belgrade, negotiations with Slovenia, and many other things. The letter was addressed to me as foreign minister, although we had a vice-president for humanitarian issues. I answered courteously based on official reports that I received from the interior ministry, although it was not my area of competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's look at your response to Elizabeth Rehn, which is a Defence exhibit -- Defence document 3D00532, and it's a letter dated 26th of June, 1996. So a few months after the letter you received from Elizabeth Rehn. And I take it you read English, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now here you inform Elizabeth Rehn that: "Regretfully the investigation of this serious crime has not yielded any results, but efforts are made to identify the perpetrators. As soon as any results are available, I will inform you of that." Now, did you ever get back to Ms. Rehn about Grubori, about any new results you might have been informed about?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I was in touch with her several times, but I don't remember if we discussed Grubori again. I received Mrs. Rehn as the foreign minister, and we co-operated very well, but humanitarian issues were not my area of work apart from the fact that as foreign minister I led negotiations with Belgrade and negotiations about the modalities of the return of refugees, but I was not in charge of humanitarian issues or investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But do you agree with me that the letter of Elizabeth Rehn we have seen a moment ago was really detailed and should have allowed you -- not you as a person, but the Croatian authorities, judicial authorities, to pick that up and do a serious investigation?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that these reports whether they are completely accurate or not should have been enough to start a serious investigation. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would there be an example of what you said yesterday, that the German -- the Croatian judiciary didn't show enough perseverance in addressing the crimes in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I was advocated a greater degree of firmness. For instance, when we received reports about Varivode which was a clear case of crime, we discussed it immediately at a cabinet session. I personally believe that every case needs to be investigated through and through and perpetrators found, and that it was very important for moral reasons, that it was important for Croatia and for her future.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the response of Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2674.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2674 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Waespi, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's a good moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I finished the Grubori incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me inquire whether you still -- whether you're still confident that you'll conclude your cross-examination in the next session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are. Then I'm looking at the other parties. As matters stand now, how much time would be needed for re-examination, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as matter stands now, I will need 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At least half an hour -- at most half an hour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was going to ask for 15 minutes, but I'll work with Mr. Mikulicic to make sure we can finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I'm regretting now that I asked before the break whether you were confident that you could finish within the next session. Mr. Granic, you know that the breaks and the pauses and meeting are often busier than the meetings themselves. Urgent Tribunal matters kept me out up to the point where even the other Judges were considering to sit under Rule 15 bis, but let's get started. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I'll be done in half an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First of all would I like to tender the document we discussed before the break which is 65 ter 4103 that related to the meeting on the 18th August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2675.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2675 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would also like to at this point to tender the excerpt from Dr. Granic's book which was -- I think it received an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was MFI'd. And if any of the other parties would like to add any portion selected by them, we'd hear from them. That's the present situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before I continue, Dr. Granic, before testifying here in The Hague, did you have a meeting -- did you talk to members of the Gotovina Defence?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I came here I talked to them while I was in Zagreb when I gave my statement and when we were making arrangements. And when we received the materials as the Bench instructed me, that was when I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I was interested in the Gotovina Defence, the Defence -- members of the Defence team of Mr. Gotovina, for instance Mr. Misetic or Mr. Kehoe or some other members of the Gotovina Defence team. Did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked with members of -- Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. Rendulic, and Mr. Tom Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you did not talk to members of the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'd like to go --

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- to an issue you discussed with Mr. Misetic about the refugees and the speech by Ms. Ogata. Let me first show you 65 ter 7508, which is an Agence France Presse report dated 26 September 1995, and it discusses the joint Croatian-Bosnian plan to second tens of thousands of Bosnian refugees in Croatia back to occupy land recently concurred from the Bosnian Serbs. And it apparently has upset humanitarian agencies. The UN officials were, and I quote, "Extremely concerned at the prospect of a mass repatriation of refugees given the unstable situation in Bosnia." And there's a comment by the UNHCR as well. Now, where you aware that there was these concerns by international organisations with Croatia forcing Bosnian refugees back into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this, after the Operation Storm and after the signing of the agreement, or to put it more precisely, after the Washington Agreement was signed there was some discussion to the effect that the Croats and the Bosniaks return to the area that were safe. I know that the international community was actively involved in this and wished that the return not be fast, but that it should proceed strictly according to the plan. I know that there were some difficulties, and personally I was in favour and I supported the positions of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that relates to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It was the return of the Croats and the Bosniaks to the territories within the federation that were safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2676.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now if we could have D690, and that's the speech of Ms. Ogata you were shown yesterday. And I'm sure you recall our discussion about that or your discussion with Mr. Misetic yesterday. Now, on page 2 of that document we have the heading of "Refoulement." Here Ms. Ogata reports the following: "In the past two months, more than 3.000 Bosnian and Muslim refugees have been forcibly returned from Croatia to towns in Western Bosnia and Herzegovina recently captured by Croat and Muslim forces such as Glamoc, Bihac, Velika Kladusa, Bosanski Petrovac, and Kluj. Some of these areas are close to front lines and are believed to be heavily mined. The next paragraph: "Moreover, recently the government of Croatia has decided to revoke the status of refugees originating from federation -- the federation and newly captured territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of a plan to begin returning them home." Now, would you agree with me what Ms. Ogata is discussing here are the so-called mass repatriations in Bosnia discussed in the article which we saw a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know precisely what issue this was and what this was all about so that I can answer all your questions relating to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'll just move on asking -- quoting a couple of parts from the Ogata speech. But my question to you right now is: What Ms. Ogata's talking about here is the same issue we have seen in the media article just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More or less it is the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Ogata went on to say: "I fully appreciate that the more than 200.000 Bosnian refugees in Croatia represent a great burden on the country's resources. However, I also strongly believe that repatriating large numbers of them at this time, when neither a comprehensive peace has been achieved, nor rehabilitation work has yet begun, would be premature. The refugees have already suffered enough in exile. Let us not compound their plight by returning them to an area which is neither safe nor ready to receive them." Would you agree that this reflects a concern about Bosnia and that the numbers are too high?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Washington Agreement, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the Federation wished that the return of refugees should begin as soon as possible, and in particular the Bosniaks were very sensitive, and they wanted the Bosniaks from Croatia not to leave to third countries, and the plans were made at the appeal and at the request of the government of the Federation for them to return as soon as possible. However, then as we can see, Ms. Ogata and the high commissariat intervened and they requested that the rules of return be strictly adhered to, and that meant that there could be no quick return until all the conditions had been met and the security was complete. Personally, I supported Ms. Ogata's position. The plans were made, and this position was fully taken into account, the position expressed here by Ms. Ogata.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And one of the concerns she had is that to a certain extent the conflict in Bosnia was still ongoing. That's why it was unsafe to send large numbers of refugees into Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the areas where the refugees were supposed to return there was no fighting any more, but it is a fact that a great part of Bosnia was occupied and that according to the assessment of Ms. Ogata there was still no conditions for all these refugees to return. Personally, I think that this was correct, and I supported this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now let's go to page 4 of the document, speech by Ms. Ogata in English, and I think Mr. Misetic drew your attention to that section where Ms. Ogata discusses three phases of refugee repatriation. And this is in the third paragraph on this page which starts with "Secondly."

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I read the last one or two sentences of that paragraph that starts with "Secondly." "Returning large numbers of refugees to areas which are not yet ready to receive them can have very serious consequences not only for the refugees themselves but for the stability in the area concerned. I am thinking particularly of the still fragile situation ... of the Federation." Now, what Ms. Ogata is talking about is -- the Federation is Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's what she was discussing in the first part of the document when we looked at these comments about Velika Kladusa, Bosanski Petrovac, and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosanski Kladusa issue is completely different, and she described it very nicely, so I would ask you to say a bit more about this. This 100.000 people related to other areas within Bosnia and Herzegovina, their return, I mean, and the problem of Kladusa was separate. The issue about Kladusa was that Mr. Abdic's forces fought, these were the forces of Bosniaks headed by Mr. Abdic, against the 5th Corps of the BH army, that is to say the official government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And after the conclusion of the operations in which Croatia supported the official government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, these refugees fled before the 5th Corps into Croatia. So they just crossed the border into Croatia. And practically on one side we had the request of the official government of Bosnia-Herzegovina that they returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on the other hand there was the wish of these people who were still under great influence of Mr. Abdic that they remain in Croatia and not return because they didn't feel safe. So we were under pressure of the official government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and eventually we decided to listen to the advice of Ms. Ogata. Germany also provided some assistance, and at that time they remained in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The only issue I was interested in was whether in your understanding Ms. Ogata was talking about events, the stability of the area in -- in Bosnia and not elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She was thinking about stability in Bosnia, in the area around Bihac, because the 5th Corps of the BH Army had won, and she had justified fears that there might be retaliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic. Let me turn to my last issue, and that's something you have discussed yesterday. You told us yesterday -- you remember when we were exploring your knowledge about events, especially about when you heard for the first time about crimes, torching, looting, killings, committed by members of the Croatian Army. You remember that discussion?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember everything I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said, and I quote you from yesterday's transcript -- unfortunately, I don't have the comprehensive numbering -- at pages 127, 128: "The first information I got as far as torching and looting is concerned that they," members of the Croatian Army, "were involved I began to receive sometime in September. I don't know exactly when. We had what we call rumours. Rumours began to reach me that there was involvement in individual cases of the army too." Now, let me show you a couple of documents. The first one is P2159, and this is a -- the witness statement which evidence of Mr. Lausic. In e-court it's paragraph 45, in English. And I can already read the last sentence of paragraph 212, and this discusses knowledge of the Croatian leadership, about crimes. The last sentence in paragraph 212: "I can say with certainty that the highest level of the military and state were informed on a daily basis of all the cases of crimes committed and military indiscipline for the entire territory of the Republic of Croatia." That's the first quote. Let me move to D49. And D49, Dr. Granic, is a very urgent report from Josko Moric to police administrations all over that area, Dalmacija. 18 August 1995. Now, here's what Mr. Moric says: "Written and oral reports by police stations and police administrations show that there are daily cases of torching of houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property in areas liberated in Operation Storm. "Most of these acts are perpetrated by individuals wearing Croatian Army uniforms. The facts indicate that these individuals are, formally and actually, members of the Croatian Army, but there are also individuals who are not members of the Croatian Army but are wrongly wearing Croatian Army uniforms." This is 18th August, 1995. It goes to the chief of police administrations, crimes committed by members of the army. And the last document is D506. This is a document as early as 9 August 1995, and it comes from Mr. Lausic, and it's addressed to Mr. Susak, Defence Minister; Zvonimir Cervenko, chief of the General Staff; Miroslav Tudjman, the director of the Croatian intelligence service; and other people including Mr. Tolj [phoen]. If we go to the second page, we see that Mr. Lausic reports that: "There are grave problems because of the large number of HV members in the settlements, and their commanders do not exert influence over them so that there are attempts at random plunder and burning of buildings." And then he proposes appropriate measures. Now, you as the foreign minister selling the Croatian state of affairs to the whole world, you were on the basis of rumours you say you received in September that army members have been involved in these crimes. That's your basis despite the fact that it was well known within the Croatian authorities, Ministry of Interior, Ministry of Defence, that almost from the outset members of the Croatian Army were involved in crimes. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as you can see, none of these memos were addressed to me. At the time, according to the constitution, we had a semi-presidential system in which I as the foreign minister reported to the president of the country about diplomacy and foreign affairs. Mr. Susak, as the defence minister, reported about Defence. Mr. Jarnjak as the interior minister reported about the internal affairs. No one meddled with anyone else's affairs. This was not allowed. I never received any memos either from the Ministry of Defence or the Ministry of the Interior except for official discussions at government meetings and other official discussions at the meeting of the VONS, or if we requested official written reports about certain specific events. I have told this Tribunal that I was personally touched very much when I heard in late August that the scope of crimes which occurred in the ground was more widespread than I had known before that, thanks to what I had heard through official reports. So this was the reason why I could not have received such information except if I had heard them officially expressed at the government meeting or at the meeting of the council for national security. And another thing, up until that time, around the month of September, it was being talked about people in uniforms. It was then that I heard that some members of the army also participated in the torching, looting, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We heard yesterday from you, and it's part of your book, that you had meetings with Mr. Susak, with Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Jarnjak, all these people, throughout August, and they never informed you, despite fact that you raised this issue with them, what information they had received from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say it very precisely, Mr. Prosecutor. It was a time when I met Mr. Susak and Mr. Jarnjak at official meetings, because simply there was too much work for me to hold any private meetings with them. This just didn't happen. It was only at official meetings, and the only situation when I requested to have a meeting with them was when I heard the information from many sources, as I said yesterday, that the scope of the problems on the ground was much greater than I had been aware of previously. That was when I requested to hold separate meetings with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The question I was asking you is whether Mr. Susak, as an example, raised with you the information he received on 9th of August, in relation to the army committing crimes. That should have been important information for you to receive when you talked to your interlocutors at the international level.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before this Honourable Court I said very precisely yesterday, and I wrote in my book exactly what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it possible then that you were completely out of tune of what was happening, that people did not inform you of what they heard or saw or were informed about what was happening, really happening, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat once again. I told what I had heard and what I knew, but now I'm saying with hindsight that Minister Susak must have believed he was capable of dealing with the problem himself on his own, but that's what I'm -- what I can say only with hindsight. You must remember that as the foreign minister I was simply elsewhere every other day dealing with foreign affairs. My primary job was communication with the international community, continuing the US peace initiative, opening talks with Belgrade. The events following Operation Storm and the crimes that occurred inflicted great damage to all my efforts, that's certain. As a human being, as the foreign minister, as a diplomat, I was inflicted. I was enraged over every torched house, over every murder. I was deeply unhappy about all that. I was doing all I could. And when I realised that this evil could not be stopped with the speed that I thought necessary, I turned to the media, and I wanted wide coverage in order to stop that evil as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Granic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic, as you know, is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Granic. Yesterday in the course of your evidence and the day before yesterday, on several occasions you mentioned the number 3 or 4.000 crimes that were prosecuted and the illegal nature of the acts that occurred after the liberation.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when Judge Orie asked you where you got that number, said you'd heard it at a cabinet session or in the media.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at an official cabinet session, and it was covered by all the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have D1339, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, we'll now see a document that has been exhibited, and it provides certain information that the Defence of accused Markac received from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was asking for 1331. I'm sorry, I saw in transcript that it was wrongly mentioned, 39. It has to be 1331. Sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Granic, through official channels we received from the Ministry of Justice a document containing the numbers for prosecutions and crimes that occurred after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you open page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the bottom we see a table showing the total number of crimes and criminal proceedings. The first line is the number of indictees and criminal acts, 3.978. The next line shows that there were 1.949 judgements; out of which 1.492 guilty verdicts, that is convictions; 179 acquittals; and 278 reversals of judgements. The statistics that we got from the Ministry of Justice, does it remind you of the sources that you used when you got that number, 3 to 4.000 crimes?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just for a reference, let me also call -- or, rather, refer to D1392, which is the white paper containing the same numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we now call D429. Mr. Granic, when you were cross-examined by the Prosecutor and questioned by the Trial Chamber, there was also the issue of the total number of refugees who returned eventually to Croatia. Let us wait for a second to see the document. This is a table made by the Ministry for Public Works and Reconstruction, department for refugees. You see that up to 2nd December 1996, total returnees were 123.469. It's in column number five from the left. Does this number correspond to what you mentioned in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we now call P2671. This exhibit that we will soon see was discussed between you and the Prosecutor, and it's a document from the 4th of September, 1995. Tudjman is quoted on the last page when he said regarding the issue of whether 150.000 Krajina Serbs may return home, President Tudjman answered it was unthinkable for all of them to return. In your answer you explained your understanding of the context, and then the question followed if military operations were still ongoing and what the security situation was. Can we see page 2 in the Croatian where the journalist asks President Tudjman, What will happen if the conflict in Eastern Slavonija cannot be ended peacefully, will there be a new offensive? Tudjman says: "Yes. In the following three months, we will do our utmost to achieve a peaceful solution, but if that is impossible, we will have no choice but to mount a new operation." Mr. Granic, at the time of this interview in September 1995, in the state political leadership was the military option still under the consideration in order to recover occupied territories?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We hoped and we believed -- let me be very pragmatic. The international community, especially the US, we hoped would help us achieve a peaceful solution, but we were obviously prepared to go for the military option if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In that political environment at the time, when the military option was still on the table, was it possible to proceed with a systematic return of refugees?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only was it impossible, but even if we had wanted to proceed we would not have received the support of the UNHCR. We had heard a moment ago from the Prosecutor about the positions of Mrs. Sadako Ogata concerning the federation. I supported them at the time. And the same was true of Croatia at the time. There was no time to think -- that was not the time to think about systematic return, only individual returns, and individual returns proceeded very intensively as you can see from that table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
