utterances.text: Could you place in the same context the events that occurred after the liberation action of Storm concerning the regrouping of the fugitive military conscripts from the occupied territories and from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Those were indisputable facts. Karadzic and Martic were boasting that they were recruiting younger refugees into the Army of Republika Srpska, that they were also setting up terrorist units, that they had created a government in exile. So at the time the possibility that a part of the Croatian territory would again be cut off by actions mounted from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was a high priority for Croatia. If I remember well, the reports I had as the foreign minister at UN Security Council sessions [as interpreted], I think that about 14.000 [as interpreted] of our soldiers were deployed on the front line facing the FR Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just if you'll give me the leeway, Mr. President. At page 48, line 7. It was interpreted as UN Security Council sessions, and I believe the witness said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness. You said: "If I remember well, the reports I had as the foreign minister at ..." some sessions. What session were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The National Security Council of Croatia. Thank you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I've just been advised by my colleagues, Your Honour, that there is also doubt on number that witness mentioned, so could we ask him again. Is it really number of 14.000 or some other number he had in mind he had mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirty thousand soldiers were deployed on the eastern border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This all being on the record, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I now ask for 3D00960.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Granic, there was also talk about a decree of the Croatian government that was later written into law, the decree on the provisional restriction over administration of abandoned property. That decree gave course to great reservations and comments. I'll show you the transcript of the 262nd session of the Republic of Croatia government from August 1995. 1st August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid this document that we are looking at the screen is not the right one that I'm looking for. This is a, let's say, summary of that government's meeting, and I was asking for the transcript of the meeting which is 3D00968. But let me check, Your Honour, just a minute, please. So we could go to the second page in English, and six page in Croatian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Granic, at this session the cabinet discussed the idea and the need to adopt a decree restricting the disposal of property. And Mr. Misetic, whom you mentioned as deputy prime minister in charge of this work is giving a statement of reasons in the first passage. I'd just like to repeat, there are several categories of property and several categories of citizens involved. Page 3 in English. And Mr. Misetic goes on to say what property this is, and he says, first of all, this is the property of the citizens of Croatia who on that notorious 17th of August, when the aggression against Croatia started, left for the occupied territories. What here does he mean when he says 17th August as the date of aggression against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17th August 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, the interpreters did not hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is clear now. So this is one category of property that was included in the decree, and then the deputy prime minister Misetic says the following in the same paragraph: "Then we are dealing here with the property of natural persons and legal entities, citizens of the then republics of Serbia and Montenegro whose property is in the territory of the Republic of Croatia." And in the next paragraph he talks about the third category which was actually the subject of discussion here, and that was the property of those citizens, primarily of those in the occupied territories, who left the Republic of Croatia after the liberation of those occupied territories. All these three categories of property are rated by this law as the property without the proprietor, as their proprietors left the Republic of Croatia. And then Mr. Misetic talks about the purpose for adopting this law. And he says the purpose of this law is to make this property subject to proper management as the good governor would do in order to avoid an unfathomable damage to this property, as well as to ensure that through the proposed fashion of management and manipulation of this property a number of Croatian citizens, primarily the Croats who were expelled by the Serbs from other areas and from other countries, would benefit from this property, primarily from the area of the former Yugoslavia to the area of the Republic of Croatia. And then if we turn the page in Croatian - the English page we have is okay - Mr. Misetic further says somewhere around the top third of the page, this is what he says: "There have been quite a few proposals and opinions. The final proposal of coordinating bodies for internal affairs and of all others who took part in the creation of this law is that all this property is to be sequestered by the Croatian state. Therefore, meaning that the State of Croatia shall be responsible for its management, rather than to state in a law or in an enactment that this is property of the Republic of Croatia." Mr. Granic, is your recollection to this -- to these events in accordance with this as it was expressed by the deputy prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My recollection is exactly the same. I'm not a lawyer, but what I know precisely and what I advocated as the foreign minister was that by this, the issue of property would not be resolved, but exclusively the protection of property at that point in time. And of course as it is noted here, there were between 25 and 30.000 refugees, mostly Croats who had been expelled from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from Republika Srpska, from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and who were in the area. And another thing that was considered was to allow them to use houses that had not been damaged in order to resolve the humanitarian problem. So the priority was only to protect property rather than to resolve the issue of the property. And I know this precisely for the following reason: After several months, on the 10th of January, 1996, I said in Belgrade that private property of refugees was inviolate, and on the 31st of August I signed the agreement on the normalisation in which this was set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Granic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I forgot something. Could I tender into the evidence the last document. It is 3D00960.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1823.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1823 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, let me clarify something because there may have been some confusion. You did not meet with the Gotovina Defence after you began your testimony. But prior to your testimony we did have a meeting, Mr. Kehoe, me, and yourself, in the offices of the Markac Defence the day you arrived in The Hague; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were asked some questions, and this is Exhibit P2675, it is a presidential transcript, and you will recall that the -- that there was a comment taken about President Tudjman speaking to his ambassadors about his views concerning Serbs in Banja Luka and -- as well as Russia's influence and how the west would also be impacted by Serbs in Banja Luka. Now, I'd like to show you or play for you an audio of a meeting between President Tudjman and Mr. Holbrooke on the 17th of September 1995. Mr. Galbraith is also present, and again it's the same topic, Serbs in Banja Luka, Russia's influence, and what President Tudjman means by this. So if we could take a listen to a broader context of that line, and then I'll ask you some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I believe this is 65 ter 1D357.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "[Interpretation] To suggest to them such a territorial division whereby Banja Luka would go to the Western part of the Federation and Tuzla to the Eastern part. And this way we'd have a civilizational and humane solution, that they are not ethnically clean. Therefore, let the Serbs remain in the Federation as well as the Muslims and the Croats in the Serbian part. Based on the reciprocal guarantees of human and ethnic equality. In that case we would have a boundary between the East and the West, between Russian and Western influence for the future, so that we wouldn't have to fear any future war."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Granic, what President Tudjman was talking about is Serbs staying in Banja Luka, but being part of the Muslim/Croat federation. And Tuzla, Bosnians, Muslims, and Croats staying in Tuzla but becoming part of the part of the Republika Srpska. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's completely accurate. If I may give you a brief comment on that. Your Honours, sometime around, I believe, the 14th or the 15th of June 1995, in Geneva, the Contact Group at the level of ministers where I was also present on behalf of the Republic of Croatia adopted a decision that in the future Bosnia and Herzegovina there will exist Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that the relation would be 51 to 49 per cent, but nothing was decided about the demarcation of borders between Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After the joint operations of the BH Army, the HVO, and the army of the Republic of Croatia, with the full support of the USA, and this was the time before the Dayton agreement, there was no agreement about borders, and President Tudjman was, therefore, talking about a very legitimate option, legitimate because there was no demarcation of borders. It was just talking in principle about the relations. And when on the 14th of October, 1995, about which I testified, when the State Secretary Christopher called me and so did embassy -- Ambassador Holbrooke to President Tudjman and told us to stop before Banja Luka. They also called President Izetbegovic and President Tudjman. It was only then that the Americans said, No, don't go for that, and we are not in fair of this option. So up until that time it was a legitimate option.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Granic, on the basis of President Tudjman's comments that what he wants is for the territory to be part of the federation, the territory of Banja Luka, but he's prepared to accept that Serbs would stay in Banja Luka -- the comment that was read to you in P2675 about how "it would be unpleasant for Croatia to have Serbs in Banja Luka and on the west like we had them 30 kilometres from Zagreb, but it is unpleasant for the west as well," is President Tudjman there referring to Serb people, or is he referring to Serb entities like the RSK and the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that context he meant drawing the borders between Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he noted, and this was a well-known opinion that he held, that the Serbs in Banja Luka were western oriented just like the Serbs in Tuzla were connected with Belgrade much stronger, and that was what Tudjman had in mind at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 65 ter 1D357 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- this was which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's the audio with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that becomes Exhibit D1824.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, you were asked quite a lot of questions about your knowledge of crimes committed by members of the Croatian Army, and I'd like to explore -- explore that topic a bit because it was put to you that either you knew about them or that other people were lying to you about this issue. So let's see if we can quickly go through that. You've already seen, and we went through this yesterday so there's no need to pull this up again, but the transcript of the conversation between Mr. Radic and President Tudjman which took place on the 22nd of August, which is Exhibit P463, at page 5 where Mr. Radic is saying that it is not the Croatian Army but the 5th echelon that is committing these crimes. If we can move to another document, which is Exhibit D426. And you will note that this is a closed-session meeting of the Croatian government on the 23rd of August. We'll wait for the English translation to come up, but, Mr. Granic, you will see at the bottom in the Croatian you were not present for this meeting, but if we turn the page in Croatian and stay on the first page in English, you'll see that present was, in fact, your then deputy minister of foreign affairs, Mr. Sanader; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And would -- if Mr. Sanader as your deputy attended a meeting, a closed-session meeting of the government, would you receive a report from him or from somebody else to you because you were absent telling you what the meeting was about or what was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was something very important, he would have told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's take a look, if we may, at English page 21, Croatian page 42. It's the bottom of the page in Croatian, the bottom paragraph, and it's the third and fourth paragraphs on the English page. Now, these are the words as recorded of the prime minister, Mr. Valentic, and speaking to the government he says: "Speeding up the procedure of solving citizenship issues, the Ministry of Administration should speed up the procedure as much as possible ..." And if we could turn the page in Croatian, please. "... of course the social and health care, as we have arranged, have to be intensified in the areas where people live regardless of their nationality. Special care has to be provided to the Serb population. There is no need to mention how important this issue is today in both political and humanitarian terms, and it has to be outspoken that all the liberators who are liberating for the third time, those are the worst, they must be prevented. After the army had passed and the war is virtually over, some fake heroes emerged who are the most dangerous for Croatia at this moment. There are places for them to fight at if they want to find" -- I think it says, "if they want to fight they should tell us, and we will send them. There are several front lines where fighters are needed, but we will not allow them to fight around Knin and around Okucani." Now, Mr. Granic, first, can you explain in case it's unclear, when the prime minister says, "those who are liberating for the third time," what is he really referring to?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who were committing crimes, and most of them were wearing Croatian Army uniforms. And I have said this a number of times. I was difficult to distinguish then because most of the people were wearing the Croatian Army uniform in this area, and I think that it was only logical that the criminals who went there in order to loot, it was easier for them to enter these areas if they were wearing uniforms. What I can also say is that the prime minister believed at the time that whoever was committing crimes was doing this against Croatia, and he never made any distinction who it was. Whoever was doing it was doing it against Croatia. Whoever was committing any crimes was working against Croatia, even those who, as he put it, went to liberate areas after they had been liberated and that they were causing the greatest damage for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that the assessment was as Mr. Valentic, the prime minister, lays out, that it was after the army had passed and the war is virtually over that that's when some "fake heroes" emerged, that that was the assessment at the time?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You'll note in the next paragraph, and -- he says -- now he's talking about the decree on property. He says: "... is very significant. We are aware of all the constitutional restrictions. You are familiar with my position. We will not allow any violence, but we have to do something. It is better to find a preliminary solution than to allow anarchy. We will find a constitutional and formal way to find a solution, a preliminary solution which will lead us to a final solution of that issue. No one can keep it under control. We do not have sufficient army and police to keep under control 30 or 40.000 apartments." Now, Mr. Granic, was that in fact one of the reasons for the property law, the fact that Croatia felt that this would improve the security of the housing that was placed under the law?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the main reason, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, would the prime minister, Mr. Valentic, would he have been able to express these kinds of views and implement policies towards fixing the security situation on the ground had that been in conflict with President Tudjman's objectives?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That would have been impossible. If he had a different opinion, then Prime Minister Valentic would go to see President Tudjman and would have told him his opinion because he was a very independent man. So this was really his sincere opinion, and it was not contrasted with what President Tudjman believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's look at another conversation on the same day. So these are now -- this is the third conversation within the two-day period. This is Exhibit D890. And you were asked several questions about whether Mr. Susak or Mr. Jarnjak were lying to you. And if we could go to page 9 in the English. This is a meeting between Minister Susak, Minister Jarnjak, and the president on the 13th of August. It's on page 9 in the English and page 17 in the Croatian. Now, at the top in Croatian and the upper middle part in the English, Mr. Jarnjak is speaking, and he says: "There's a huge problem that now after Storm and after Flash" -- he says, "however, there's a huge problem that now after Storm and after Flash there are now again so many weapons in private hands, explosives uncontrolled, that is simply -- I don't know. We will now pass this law, and we will have to launch a massive campaign for the return of these weapons. Look, I know of rifles, automatic ones, anything you want." And Minister Susak says: "Mr. President, here in a house, a private house, to get in there and find 100 kilogrammes of explosives, that's nothing." Now, if we could turn the page in English, please, and in Croatian. And then towards the bottom in English. Actually, if we could scroll up to the top in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK SAYS
utterances.text: "We are doing this without a law. What we're dealing -- what we're doing with the mobilisation, because we're simply taking away by force ... there is no law saying what you're allowed to do and what you're not. "There was a law stating what is allowed and what is not," this is Mr. Jarnjak, "but the problem is that nobody will report, nobody will report anybody. You have plenty of grenades." Now, if we scroll down a bit and turn the page in Croatian, please. Mr. Susak then tells the president: "But they hand in the weapons they were issued officially. But, Mr. President, what they had now in the operation, especially the home guard and the reserves, they wouldn't record anything they took. We gave him a rifle, and he will return the rifle to us. But the fact that he took two more on top of that, that's something we have no record of." Now, Mr. Granic, the three conversation I've now referenced to you took place over a period of two days, the 22nd and 23rd of August. All of them are private conversations not for public consumption, not to deceive the international community. Was it in the fact the case that the assessment of the Croatian government which you were reporting at the time was that these were being committed after Operation Storm by persons not under the control of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I see these talks for the first time, but I'm familiar with the context, and the context is quite accurate. That means there were problems with demobilisation and the retrieval of weapons, there were many, many weapons out of any control. And of course these men were wearing uniforms, they had weapons plenty, and it was easy for them to get together into criminal gangs. That was a huge problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have approximately ten minutes of questions left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll first have a break, Mr. Misetic. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, you were asked some questions about Bihac, and you were shown the, as Mr. Waespi referred to it, the famous Brioni transcript. The suggestion that was put to you was that Bihac had become a pretext by the 31st of August, and I'd like to ask you some questions on the following: First of all, were you aware that Mr. Akashi had, on the night before the Brioni meeting, sent a fax to President Tudjman where he had essentially claimed that Mr. Martic had agreed to a six point agreement which included that he would withdraw from Bihac. Were you aware that the president had received such a communication from Mr. Akashi the night before the Brioni meeting which would be the 30th of July?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only in general terms about it, and President Tudjman told me about it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, were you aware that in fact Mr. Akashi had not reached an agreement because Mr. Martic had backed out of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And for the reference of the parties and the Chamber, this is the testimony of Mr. Akashi at transcript page 21690, beginning at line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That in fact Mr. Akashi had sent that message to President Tudjman even though he knew at the time that Mr. Martic had not agreed to the six-point plan including the withdrawal of his forces from the Bihac area? Did you subsequently learn that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had precise information that Mr. Martic was not intending to accept any kind of agreement, that his intention was to join Karadzic's forces and move forward to capture the occupied territory of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Granic, Mr. Galbraith testified in this case, and an audio of his meeting with President Tudjman on the 1st of August, which would be the day after the Brioni meeting, was played in court, and this is at transcript page 8 -- sorry. Transcript page 5029, beginning at line 8. And the audio shows that Mr. Galbraith had reported to President Tudjman the day after the Brioni meeting: "Today, however, we see little sign that the Serbs are withdrawing from their siege of Bihac, little sign that they are honouring previous agreements, that is, the oil -- opening the oil pipeline, little sign that they are engaged on the issues that you have raised, opening the railroad connection or beginning negotiations on political summit, and little sign that they are prepared to allow UNCRO to exercise its full mandate, and if so, we have no immediate optimism about negotiations on a political settlement." Now, were you aware, in fact, that after the Brioni meeting, the day after, the ambassador to the United States advised President Tudjman that the United States saw little sign that the RSK Serbs were withdrawing from their siege of Bihac and little sign that they were honouring previous agreements? Were you aware that the ambassador had told the president that?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am aware. President Tudjman told me so himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the decision to actually launch Operation Storm was reached at the VONS meeting on the 3rd of August and not the Brioni meeting on the 31st of August -- 31st of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: By that time, I believe you've already testified, but let's confirm, by that time Bihac was in fact one of the strategic objectives of launching Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of very important strategic objectives. I, as the foreign minister, was in daily contact either with the foreign minister Sacirbey or with Haris Silajdzic who was the prime minister or with President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic. And the final topic is this issue of Mrs. Ogata, the UNHCR, and the turn of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could please have on the screen Exhibit D690 again, please. And if we could again go to page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were shown the portion in the paragraph that begins "Secondly," and in the middle of the page there's the following two sentences: "Returning large numbers of refugees to areas which are not ready to receive them can have very serious consequences not only for the refugees themselves but for the stability in the area concerned. I am thinking particularly of the still fragile situation in the area of the Federation." Now, when you were asked about whether Mrs. Ogata meant -- was she exclusively referring to the federation in your understanding of what UNHCR's policies were in terms of when large numbers of refugees should be repatriated, or was this a principle of UNHCR that applied to all of the republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite certainly it applied equally to the federation and the Republic of Croatia. Mrs. Sadako Ogata treated them equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And on this point as someone who dealt extensively with the issue -- well, let me ask you the question. As minister of foreign affairs you've talked about you dealt with the issue of refugee returns. You were familiar with that issue as it connected to -- as that issue is interconnected throughout the countries of the former Yugoslavia. In other words, the issue of refugee returns to Croatia was related to the issue of refugee returns to Bosnia, to Serbia, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As deputy prime minister, I worked intensively for accommodating refugees and displaced persons for almost two years. As a foreign minister, I discussed the topic frequently, although Professor Albert Rebic, who was a member of the cabinet and directly in charge of displaced persons and refugees was the main person dealing with it. But since this was often the topic of international discussions, I was well-versed with the whole issue and the problems involved as a foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D691, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, this is a record of the meeting of the Security Council on the 5th of September, 2002, and I'd like to use this just to discuss the principles that we've discussed now, and this will be my last question. If we could go to page 5 in this document, please. The discussion is about Kosovo. It is three years after the conclusion of hostilities in Kosovo, and this is an address to the Security Council by the assistant -- Assistant Secretary-General for peacekeeping operations, Mr. Annabi, A-n-n-a-b-i. And if we could scroll down, please. If you look on your screen, Mr. Granic, on the left-hand column,

utterances.speaker: MR. ANNABI SAYS
utterances.text: "In this context, recent statements by Kosovo Serb internally displaced persons that they are planning to block the crossing points on the administrative boundary line with Kosovo later this month if they are not allowed to return en masse are cause for concern. Although the impatience of internally displaced persons is understandable, given the still delicate state of intercommunal relations, any action along those lines would only be counter-productive and would be harmful to the return process." The next paragraph says: "There cannot be artificial mass return. UNMIK's return policy is based on the right of individual return in an organised way so that it can be sustainable. This requires careful preparation on the ground to ensure that the physical infrastructure - meaning houses, employment, and access to public services - is in place to welcome the returnees. It also requires a careful handling of relations with the neighbouring Kosovo Albanian communities to diminish the potential for return-related security incidents." Now, you were -- it was put to you this morning by Mr. Waespi that the Croatian plan was passed in June 1998, and it was suggested to you that this was an unreasonable delay in enacting this Croatian government programme. We see here that even three years after the Kosovo conflict was over the United Nations itself was opposed to mass return, and instead was espousing certain principles in the Security Council. Were these the principles upon which Croatia's return policy were based as outlined by Mr. Annabi concerning Kosovo? Are these international principles?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the very same principles that Mrs. Sadako Ogata referred to. And when we were making the programme, we were making it together with the UNHCR and with the international community. Of course the international community was impatient for as many people to return as soon as possible, but we stuck to the recommendations of the UNHCR. And there's another thing. As this report clearly says, it was necessary also to achieve an internal consensus. That was not an easy thing to do. A consensus that the time has come for massive returns. And I believe that at that time the unanimous consensus in Croatia was finally reached that an organised massive return of refugees is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Any questions from the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I would have a few questions for you. You remember that you were asked about what President Tudjman said during a meeting with Mr. Holbrooke, Mr. Clark, and Mr. Galbraith. Could I have P449, page 17 English, page 33 B/C/S. I think you explained to us that President Tudjman, when saying that he'd be very content if about 10 per cent of them returned, that he meant to say at least 10 per cent, not more than 10 per cent. That's -- and you explained that you could interpret this on the basis your knowledge of the thoughts of President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take you -- no. Let me -- you also told us that human rights, that it was always intended that human rights would be observed in relation to minorities, including Serbs. Is that also correctly understood? It's very much a --

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take you to -- could I take you to P461, page 54 in the B/C/S. And I'm not interested at this moment in the English version, I would say for obvious reasons. This page 54 out of 64? Could we then move to page 55. Could I invite you to read the portion at the top of the page where Mr. Susak is speaking, and then after that to read the words of President Tudjman after that. Just read them for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you comment on what President Tudjman says here in relation to human rights.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting, so I'm not the best person to comment. I think this is a transcript from Brioni, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only what I discussed myself in the break with President Tudjman, and I know one thing, that even our friends in the world were saying -- not the Americans, but let's say the Germans, they were saying we don't have the forces for a rapid military operation. The president talked to the soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, if you want to say at any later stage something you discussed during the break, that's fine. But I'm asking you your comments of this part of the transcript in relation to the words used by President Tudjman. And if you would like to add anything at a later stage, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president -- and I repeat I wasn't there at the meeting. The discussion was about a flyer inviting local Serbs to stay and guaranteeing their civil rights. Quite certainly that was not -- it was, in fact, a time before a military operation that had yet to be won. I cannot really comment, because in my discussions with Tudjman, it was never questioned that we would guarantee civil rights to the Serbs. I cannot say any more because I did not attend that meeting. And this thing, I guarantee ostensibly civil rights, that that's not something that Tudjman ever told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do understand his words then, although you explain to us that this comes as a surprise that President Tudjman here expresses that the rights of Serbs might or would not be observed. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. This is a discussion before the military operation with the military leaders. It's not a discussion with the government or the foreign minister or with those officials in charge of human rights or international conventions and treaties. This is a discussion with the army. Since wasn't there, I can't say any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have seen these words, would you have spoken with President Tudjman, and would you have explained to him that you could not agree with this? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had seen this or if I had been there, then I would have said, "Mr. President, we have to honour human and civil rights very honestly and sincerely." That's how I would react in any other situation. But I think -- I mean, you see this is a different context, and this is a sentence that's really cut off, that trails off. I cannot say with any certainty what President Tudjman meant 15 years ago. I think he was speaking exclusively about a flyer that may help achieve military victory. As for human rights, if anyone in my hearing ever said ostensibly in connection with human rights, my reaction would always have been the same. We have had honour human rights always, everywhere, and that's our supreme principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which would contradict ostensibly observing human rights.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that the president certainly didn't mean that we would ostensibly respect human rights. I think this sentence belongs in the context of a conversation to which I was not present, and I cannot give any further comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, apparently the president used the word "toboze." Is there anything you would like to tell us about the use of that word by the president? Did he often use that? Do you have no recollection of him using it?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he used it sometimes. I said that the president was not a diplomat, although he was a statesman. He was an expert in the modern understanding of human rights, but it's indisputable that every move I made -- and I did all I did to protect the Serb minority and all minorities, the protection of property and the return of refugees. Every movie made was supported by Tudjman. And as for his communication skills, he had been an outcast from public life for a -- for a long time, and he was not an expert in international treaties or human rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it true that you earlier said that he was not an expert in the modern understanding of human rights, because on the transcript it appears as if he was an expert, but you told us he was not an expert. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and I stand by it, the president was not a diplomat, and he was not an expert in modern understanding of human rights, but he had a very good basic understanding that the highest standards of human rights must be guaranteed to Serbs in Croatia. He understood that very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea, if you know, please tell us, what was good about the confusion that was apparently the chaos that was apparently sought? If you know. If you've got no idea, then please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I know nothing about this. I cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From any other conversation, because you were not present here, have you gained any understanding of how showing people the way out would encourage them not to leave?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about the session itself except that it was held and that President Tudjman discussed the military readiness of the army to execute the task of liberating the occupied territory of Croatia and emerging at the borders as well as the military assistance to Bihac. And of course the third point was the assistance to the US peace initiative. Now, I spoke to the president myself that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Until now you have told us what the meeting was about. I asked you whether you had any conversation. So I see that you now come to that point. Please proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to him that day myself. The president asked me to give him a precise evaluation at the international level, the US evaluation, and the evaluations of the leading states in the world. I shared with him those appraisals, and I said that the presidential statement will be heard at the Security Council, and I repeated this: We have to honour the international conventions on the laws of warfare. We have to respect civilians. We have to respect the UNCRO soldiers, and the operation has to be swift. That's the same thing our friends are recommending, especially the US. And I repeated it at least twice. President, everyone will have as much respect for us as we have respect for international convictions and the international humanitarian law. And he said, Okay. I'll convey this to the soldiers and to Minister Susak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand this answer that you had no conversation in which, as I asked you, that you gained any understanding of how showing people the way out would encourage them not to leave, because I do not find any response to that question in your answer. May I take you now to P463.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is correct, Your Honour. I did not talk to him about this, and I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- could I take you to P463. Page 14 in the B/C/S and page 10 in English. Now, let me see. Did I make a mistake? Is this 46 -- there we are. This is a transcript of a conversation between the president and Mr. Radic. Could I ask you to read the words spoken by Mr. Radic, but perhaps we should move to page 15. No. Perhaps I'll invite you to start reading at -- no. We are here at 14. Could we move to page 13. When I'm talking about pages, I'm referring to e-court pages, and this seems to be a problem. Could you start reading the observations at the bottom of -- next page, 14 e-court. Could I ask you to read the last portions of what Mr. Radic said. Once you finish this page, please tell me so we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can move to the next page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier told us that because of your knowledge of the thoughts of President Tudjman, you could interpret his reference to being happy with 10 per cent to return, that that would be -- not less than 10 per cent. The text you've just read where Mr. Radic said: "We should by no means let more than 10 per cent of Serbs be here ever again, because that's where we were cut off." Where the president said "not even 10 per cent," I have some difficulties in reconciling your interpretation of what President Tudjman said to Mr. Holbrooke, Clark, and Galbraith with what he says to Mr. Radic. Could you help me out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Let --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we established yesterday what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to -- yes. Nevertheless, would I like to put this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This was, of course, a private conversation between Jure Radic and the president that I was not familiar with. This is the first time I see the transcript. But in the transcript it says very clearly that Jure Radic says that in that area there should be no more than 10 per cent of Serbs, rather than only 10 per cent of Serbs or less should return to the Republic of Croatia. This is a big difference. Jure Radic is saying here that as many Croats as possible should be returned to this area so that the number of Serbs in the area would be less than 10 per cent. And, frankly, there was not a session of the government or the VONS, the security for the protection of national security, where this was mentioned. These are the positions at the time of the minister who was in charge of demographic reconstruction and who believed that this area that had been vacated by both Serbs and Croats should be repopulated by as many Croats as possible. That was the issue, rather than the issue of return of Serbs to Croatia, but that as many Croats should be brought to this area as possible. And of course, these were the views that were never realised, and there was never any session of the Croatian government where any conclusion of this kind was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the percentage of Serbs in the area referred to before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area, and it was an area with mixed population, so probably there were equal per cents. I don't know exactly, but I suppose that in the wider area there were equal numbers of Serbs and Croats, perhaps even some more Serbs. It depends on the area that Jure Radic had in his mind. And I don't know which exact area he had in his mind here, but it was an area with a mixed population of Serbs and Croats. I don't know exactly because I cannot see from this which area he had in mind and how large an area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do the words "We should by no means let more than 10 per cent of Serbs be here ever again," is that just mathematics, or is it more?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this only refers to mathematics. Obviously, Jure Radic had an idea that as many Croats as possible should inhabit this empty area. And let me also say that none of these ideas ever came into being, and no topic similar to this one was ever addressed at the meeting of the Croatian government. There were discussions about the return of Croats from the world, but I should note that the Croats who had fled Serbia, most of them ended up in big cities and the majority of them in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say that limiting Serbs to live in the area referred to by the number of 10 per cent never was government policy.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. The government never made any such decision nor discussed that, at least as far as I can remember, and so far I have quite a good recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you agree that from what we read here that the -- President Tudjman was even more strict where he said "not even 10 per cent"? Even if it's not -- I'm now talking about his personal attitude and his personal approach to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, I'm commenting on something that I see for the first time now. However, I know that President Tudjman had the idea that as many Croats as possible from around the world should return to Croatia once an Independent State of Croatia was constituted. That was one of his sincere ideas that never came into being in any respect. Another idea was that the area that was empty, and that continues to be empty to this day, should be populated by as many Croats as possible. This is another idea that never came into being in any way, but it was not an idea or -- and it did not have anything to do with preventing the return of Serbs to Croatia. He just wanted more Croats to live there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's -- if you have a room where there's place for ten people, if I say I want nine places for ethnicity A, wouldn't it true that there's only one place left for the other ethnicity? I mean, I'm just trying to understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judge, this is outside the context of the transcript. If we could refer to the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking -- I'm testing the reasoning of this witness, not specifically in relation to this. Please proceed, Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been an empty space. It was empty, and it is still empty. It's poorly developed economically. And the president's thoughts were certainly focused on strategic issues, because this was an area where the Serbs in Croatia had rebelled. This was an area that had seen 14.000 casualties and 36.000 wounded. And the first assessment was that the damage was 37 billion US dollars. And when president was thinking about this, this was what he had in mind, rather than that he was against the return of the Serbs. These were his thoughts. That is what, I suppose, the president was thinking. And after the Operation Storm and after some time, we introduced some areas where special care was needed, where we stimulated both Croats and Serbs to live in these areas. The taxation was reduced. There were special stimulants introduced in the municipalities, and still it did not contribute to an increase of the number of Croats who would return to these areas, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers, Mr. Granic. Mr. Waespi, you were the last for re-cross, and as often, the Chamber put the questions. Any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks for the invitation. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions from any of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I may quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In we could limit to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Then at least I'm saying yes, but I'm hoping to get the support from those assisting us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, the transcript on the screen, you were asked about limited space. And if we look at what's actually discussed, we talked about this yesterday. First of all, the territory in question is the Petrova and Zrinska Gora, which you circled on the map; but secondly, what Radic says is, "There where we have to establish some kind of a city sooner or later." Mr. Radic is actually talking about not using -- not simply using the available facilities there, but actually building a city right in that location, and it's -- because it's a strategic area of Croatia where it could easy be cut off and was cut off during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's what the first area to be cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with Knin, that was the first area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's put everything back in the context of this war. And let me point out something that General Mrksic testified about when he was here in front of the Chamber, and he said this three times. I'll refer to it just once, which is at transcript page 1905, line 20, is where it begins. And General Mrksic's theme was: "We didn't have an army and a people; we had an armed people." Now that was the perception of -- two weeks after Operation Storm of many in the Croatian government; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about the Brioni meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if I could please have Exhibit D1454, please. Mr. Granic, what's going to be shown to you is a transcript of the VONS meeting on the 3rd of August. You are present at that meeting. Also present is every important minister of the government as well as the prime minister, and you've already testified this is where the decision to launch Operation Storm happened. We talked about civil rights, toboze, civil rights, et cetera. But let's quickly take a look at what was discussed about that issue. If we can go to page 5 in the English, please. This is -- and I'm going to go through this quickly, Mr. Granic. This is where Mr. Zuzul talks about the American conditions and the need to protect civil rights. If we could go to page 8, please. Towards the bottom Mr. Jarnjak is speaking, and he says -- I'm sorry, this is where you were speaking, and you also convey the messages concerning the need for protection and respect of human rights. That's there. If we go -- there are several other entries, and I'll just for the record to save time, they are at page 9, page 11, and page 12 of the -- this transcript concerning the issue of protection of human rights. Mr. Susak in the transcript says that he had met with Mr. Jarnjak and the security plan was prepared. And if we go to page 22, please. The president there says, towards the bottom: "Very well let's go to work. I haven't heard the opinion on this. I said I thought I should address the Serb population. We would call the Serbs to lay down their weapons. At the same time, we could say that we would vouch for their civil rights, and after that the implementation of the elections in the spirit of the law and so forth. We would also tell the international community that the Serbs do not accept a peaceful solution. So do you think that it would be sufficient to address only the Serbs? I have to sign that appeal to them." Then there's people interrupting saying, "Only the Serbs for now." Now, the meeting of VONS, Mr. Granic, the only -- as it concerns civil rights, the only discussion was about protecting security, providing security, and appealing for people to stay, and guaranteeing their civil rights; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And I remember well this meeting, and I said myself that our friends from the world are mentioning this as the priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Last question: Have you ever seen a document of any kind from any ministry, police, army, anywhere, an order that would indicate that the Croatian government was issuing orders or implementing plans to do anything other than protect and guarantee civil rights?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That doesn't arise of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to some extent it does, but at the same time -- please answer the question, Mr. Granic. It could be a short answer. Yes or a no would do, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never seen anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, for spending quite a couple of days with us and for having answered all the questions that were put to you and by the parties and by the Bench, and I'm happy that you're able to leave on this Friday, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that at this moment there's any procedural issue to be raised. Therefore, we then adjourn, and we will resume on Monday, the 23rd of November, 9.00, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.52 p.m.,
